lead: A quadratic form turns into a sum of squares after a change of variables. The signs of those squares, not their sizes, classify the form. Count positive squares p, negative squares q, and zero squares z. Then rank = p + q. The index is p (number of positive squares) in the convention used here; some books take the index as the number of negative squares instead. The signature is p − q. These numbers stay fixed under any nonsingular change of variables, a fact called Sylvester's law of inertia. Engineers use them to test definiteness of energy and stiffness matrices, and to classify conics in coordinate geometry.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.6 for reduction to squares, plus basic conic sections from coordinate geometry.

blocks.text: Start with a real quadratic form Q(x) = xTAx, where A is symmetric. A nonsingular change x = Py gives Q = Σ ciyi2. The coefficients ci can be positive, negative, or zero. Count each type: p positive, q negative, z zero. The total number of variables is n = p + q + z. The rank of the form is rank(A) = p + q. The index is p under the convention used here: index = number of positive squares. Some books call p the positive index and q the negative index. The signature is p − q. Some syllabi write signature as the pair (p, q); check the convention before you answer. Sylvester's law of inertia says p, q, and z do not change when the change of variables is nonsingular. Different reductions may give different coefficients, but the sign counts stay the same. For example, Q = 2u2 − 5v2 + 0w2 has p = 1, q = 1, z = 1, rank = 2, index = 1, signature = 0.

blocks.where: ci are real canonical coefficients; yi are new variables; p counts positive coefficients; q counts negative coefficients; z counts zero coefficients.

blocks.text: The sign counts give a quick classification. A form is positive definite when Q > 0 for every nonzero vector. That happens exactly when p = n, so q = z = 0. It is negative definite when p = 0 and q = n. A semidefinite form allows zeros at nonzero vectors. Positive semidefinite means q = 0 and z > 0; negative semidefinite means p = 0 and z > 0. An indefinite form has both p > 0 and q > 0. Then Q takes both signs. A signature of 0 alone does not prove definiteness: x2 − y2 has p = 1, q = 1, signature = 0, but it is indefinite.

For the general second-degree equation ax2 + 2hxy + by2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, study the quadratic part ax2 + 2hxy + by2. Its matrix is [[a, h], [h, b]]. Here p is the number of positive eigenvalues and q is the number of negative eigenvalues of this 2×2 matrix. Definite gives an ellipse, or an imaginary ellipse (no real points at all), or a single point (one real point). Indefinite gives a hyperbola, or a pair of intersecting lines. Semidefinite with one zero eigenvalue gives a parabola, or parallel lines, or no real locus. The discriminant h2 − ab helps: h2 − ab < 0 means the two eigenvalues have the same sign, so the quadratic part is definite and the curve is an ellipse type; h2 − ab = 0 means it is semidefinite; h2 − ab > 0 means it is indefinite. Translation and rotation details are in Chapter 4.6.

Write A. Reduce Q to a sum of squares, or find the eigenvalues of A. List every coefficient with its sign. Count p, q, z. Compute rank = p + q, index = p, signature = p − q. State your convention in one line. For a conic, apply the counts to the quadratic part only. Then name the possible real shape. If the question asks for the nature, the signs are enough; you do not need to draw the curve. If it asks for the centre or axes, complete the square.

items: Write the symmetric matrix A of the quadratic form.
Reduce to Σ ciyi2 by completing squares or by orthogonal diagonalization.
Count p positive, q negative, z zero coefficients.
Report rank = p + q, index = p, signature = p − q.
Classify definiteness from the signs; for conics use the 2×2 quadratic part.

figure.caption: For Q = x2 + 4y2 − z2, two positive squares and one negative square fix rank, index and signature. The same signs make the form indefinite. A separate conic x2 + 4y2 = 4 has p = 2, q = 0 and is an ellipse.

spec.title: Inertia for Q
spec.aria: For Q = x² + 4y² − z², two positive squares and one negative square give p = 2, q = 1, z = 0, so rank 3, index 2, signature 1 and an indefinite form. A separate conic x² + 4y² = 4 has p = 2, q = 0 and is an ellipse.

examples.question: For Q(x, y, z) = x2 + 4y2 − z2, find the rank, index, signature and definiteness using index = number of positive squares and signature = p − q. Also classify the conic x2 + 4y2 − 4 = 0.
steps: The matrix is diagonal: A = diag(1, 4, −1).
The coefficients are 1, 4, −1. So p = 2 positive squares, q = 1 negative square, z = 0 zero squares.
p > 0 and q > 0, so the form is indefinite.
For the conic, the quadratic part is x2 + 4y2. Its matrix is [[1, 0], [0, 4]], with eigenvalues 1 and 4. Both are positive, so p = 2, q = 0.
The equation is x2 + 4y2 = 4, that is x2/4 + y2/1 = 1, an ellipse.
examples.answer: The form has rank 3, index 2 and signature 1, and is indefinite; the conic is an ellipse.
examples.check:
coeffs = [1, 4, -1]
p = sum(1 for c in coeffs if c > 0)
q = sum(1 for c in coeffs if c < 0)
z = sum(1 for c in coeffs if c == 0)
rank = p + q
index = p
signature = p - q
print(rank)
print(index)
print(signature)
print(q)
print(z)

traps: Index and signature conventions vary: here index counts positive squares and signature is p − q. Some books use the pair (p, q) as signature. State your convention.
Signs decide the type, not sizes. 100x2 − y2 is indefinite even though the positive coefficient is large.
rank = p + q, not the number of variables. Zero squares reduce rank.
Definiteness needs all nonzero vectors. Checking only the diagonal entries can fail when cross terms such as xy are present.
For a conic, one zero eigenvalue means semidefinite; that gives a parabola or parallel lines, not automatically a parabola.

quiz.q: Define index and signature for a quadratic form using p positive and q negative canonical coefficients.
quiz.a: Index = p, the number of positive squares. Signature = p − q under the stated convention.

quiz.q: Write the sign-count condition for a positive definite form in n variables.
Why does Sylvester's law of inertia matter when two different reductions give different coefficients?
quiz.a: The actual coefficients may change, but the counts p, q, z stay the same for every nonsingular change. So rank, index, signature and definiteness are properties of the form, not of one reduction.

quiz.q: For Q = 2x2 − 3y2 + 0z2, find p, q, z, rank, index, signature and definiteness.
quiz.a: p = 1, q = 1, z = 1. rank = 2, index = 1, signature = 0. Since p > 0 and q > 0, the form is indefinite.
The quadratic part has positive coefficients 4 and 9, so p = 2, q = 0. It is definite. The equation is x2/9 + y2/4 = 1, an ellipse.

quiz.q: A quadratic form in 3 variables has rank 2 and signature 0. What are the possible p, q, z values and the definiteness?
quiz.a: rank 2 means p + q = 2. signature 0 means p − q = 0. So p = 1, q = 1. Then z = 3 − 2 = 1. The form is indefinite, with one zero square.

quiz.q: A real symmetric 3×3 matrix has eigenvalues 2, 0, −5. Find rank, index, signature and definiteness, and explain whether the form can be positive semidefinite.
quiz.a: p = 1, q = 1, z = 1. rank = 2, index = 1, signature = 0. It is indefinite, not positive semidefinite, because q = 1 is not zero.

beyond: Not for the exam. In optimization, a Hessian's positive definiteness at a critical point identifies a local minimum. In control theory, Lyapunov functions use positive definite energy. In machine learning, kernel matrices are positive semidefinite. In computer graphics, conic classification helps draw curves. Search "Sylvester's law of inertia", "Hessian positive definite", and "quadratic form signature".
